newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sink or swim, Russian government tells industry.
newsitem.headline: Sink or swim, Russian government tells industry.

text.p: Russia will let ailing, old-fashioned companies sink, withdrawing state support from managers who do not embrace reforms, a deputy economy minister said on Thursday.
He also promised to strengthen shareholders' rights.
"Only reformed companies will be eligible for state support, -- that will be a stimulus," Deputy Economy Minister Sergei Vasilyev told a news conference.
The ministry will complete a list of reform criteria, to be approved by the government, in the next two weeks. Companies which do not meet government standards will not get help, he said.
A detailed plan of industrial reform will be ready within a month, he added.

Vasilyev said industrial reform hinged on improving shareholder rights, training management and making companies more worthy of investment, in part by improving the flow of information from companies.
"Potential investors do not know the real situation at companies -- even the management does not necessarily know."
Foreign investors have by and large stayed out of Russia, risking only a few billion dollars since reforms began.
Vasilyev said the Russian economy had stabilised and reformers could now focus on structural improvements.
"We need to move from the macroeconomic level to the microeconomic level -- the level of companies."
A government statement said 42 percent of Russian industrial enterprises had lost money in the first 10 months of last year, a rise from 35 percent in the same period a year earlier.
Losses in the industrial, building and transport sectors rose 2.6 in that period on a year ago, totalling 47.5 trillion roubles ($8.3 billion) in the first 10 months, it said.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Thursday pointed to rising gross domestic product, an indicator of a country's output, in January and February, which he said was the first sign of growth in five years of economic reform.
But many economists say the state had quietly changed the methodology of its statistics and thus produced the change, which was less than one percent each month.
Vasilyev said criteria would also be developed to rate managers in an effort to bring about change among Russia's industrial old guard.
A study by Rutgers University released this week showed that three quarters of chief executives at leading Russian companies had been replaced by their own deputies.
"Most are not professionally prepared to manage," Vasilyev said of company leadership.
He said the government was also preparing orders and decrees to speed land privatisation for companies and lower tariffs from natural monopolies, another major reform goal.
The government would reduce and sell its stakes in many companies, part of a move to give shareholders a bigger, stronger voice in running companies, he added.
"Companies which infringe shareholders' rights will not get government support," he said. ($ = 5726 Russian Roubles)
